Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- British Prime Minister Gordon Brown's wife, Sarah, wore an outfit from designer Britt Lintner to greet President Obama and his wife, Michelle, while Michelle Obama wore J.Crew, according to spokeswomen for both sides. Sarah Brown, left, wears a dress from an American designer. Michelle Obama wears J.Crew. Both women later changed and wore other designer outfits for the formal pre-G-20 summit dinner at 10 Downing Street, the British prime minister's official residence. Wednesday morning, Sarah Brown wore a one-of-a-kind navy dress with red lining by the American-born Lintner, a spokeswoman for 10 Downing Street said. The designer specially made the dress in navy for Brown, but retails the garment in black for $720, Lintner said. Michelle Obama's outfit included a $158 green skirt and $298 bead and rhinestone cardigan from J.Crew, the store's Web site showed. Brown also wore a pair of Astley Clarke earrings, according to a spokeswoman from 10 Downing Street. The Astley Clarke Web site sells earrings from less than $100 to more than $10,000. The first ladies' choices of outfits during this summit are being closely watched by the world's media, both in terms of style and comparative cost. Both women pay for all of their clothes themselves and receive no clothing allowance, according to spokeswomen for both sides. Lintner first designed a dress for Brown for the British Fashion Council Awards in November 2007, Lintner said. She sells to clients only through her West London studio and said she started her company out of frustration over the selection of workwear available for women. Although the clothes are expensive, she said, they are made to last. This is not the first time Michelle Obama has chosen an "off the rack" outfit. She has worn J.Crew before, including in American Vogue. When appearing on "The Tonight Show" with Jay Leno, she wore a J.Crew ensemble, on which she commented, "You get some good stuff online." After the photo call, Obama and Brown visited Maggie's Cancer Caring Center, where Brown is a patron. The spouses of the G-20 leaders have several events scheduled during their stay in London. On Tuesday, Brown will be host of a dinner for G-20 spouses. The dinner will take place at No. 11 Downing Street, the London residence of the chancellor of the exchequer, while the G-20 leaders take a working dinner next door at No. 10. As well as the spouses of the G-20 leaders, prominent women in British sport, arts, fashion, charity and business are also expected to attend. Downing Street has said those invited are "all intended to show off British talent." Those invited include "Harry Potter" author J.K. Rowling, supermodel Naomi Campbell and Olympic gold medal runner Kelly Holmes. Downing Street sources said Michelle Obama will be seated between Holmes and Rowling. The spouses also will visit the Royal Opera House in Covent Garden, London. They are expected to watch some short performances of opera and ballet, the Prime Minister's Press Office said.

LONDON, England (CNN) -- When Sarah Brown, wife of British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, greeted President Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama, she chose a piece by designer Britt Lintner, while Mrs. Obama opted for J.Crew attire, according to representatives from both camps.

The image shows Sarah Brown on the left in her American-designer dress, with Michelle Obama in her J.Crew ensemble. Later that evening, both women changed into different designer looks for the formal dinner preceding the G-20 summit, held at 10 Downing Street—the Prime Minister's official residence.

According to a 10 Downing Street representative, Mrs. Brown's Wednesday morning ensemble was a unique navy dress with red lining, crafted by American-born designer Lintner. While Lintner typically sells this design in black for $720, she created a special navy version exclusively for Brown.

Meanwhile, the J.Crew website revealed that Mrs. Obama's outfit consisted of a $158 green skirt paired with a $298 beaded and rhinestone-embellished cardigan. A Downing Street spokeswoman also noted that Brown accessorized with Astley Clarke earrings—a brand whose website offers pieces ranging from under $100 to over $10,000.

Global media outlets have been scrutinizing the fashion choices of both first ladies throughout the summit, analyzing everything from style sensibilities to price comparisons. Representatives for both women confirmed that neither receives a clothing budget or allowance—all their outfits are purchased with personal funds.

Lintner explained that her professional relationship with Brown began in November 2007, when she designed a dress for the British Fashion Council Awards. The designer, who operates exclusively through her West London studio, said she launched her business after growing frustrated with the limited workwear options available to women. She emphasized that despite the high price points, her garments are built for longevity.

This wasn't Michelle Obama's first foray into ready-to-wear fashion. She has previously donned J.Crew pieces, including for a feature in American Vogue. During an appearance on "The Tonight Show" with Jay Leno, she wore another J.Crew combination and remarked, "You get some good stuff online."

Following their photo session, Obama and Brown made a visit to Maggie's Cancer Caring Center, an organization for which Brown serves as patron.

Throughout their London stay, the G-20 leaders' spouses have a packed schedule of engagements. Sarah Brown is set to host a dinner for the visiting spouses on Tuesday at 11 Downing Street, the residence of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, occurring simultaneously with the leaders' working dinner next door at No. 10.

Beyond the G-20 spouses themselves, the guest list includes notable British women from sports, arts, fashion, philanthropy, and business sectors. # London Bridges Old and New: A City's Enduring Story

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — As one of the world's most historically rich and culturally influential cities, London continues to captivate visitors and residents alike with its unique blend of ancient heritage and modern innovation.

Founded by the Romans nearly two thousand years ago as Londinium, the city has grown from a small settlement along the River Thames into a global metropolis of over 9 million people. Its skyline tells this story vividly—the medieval Tower of London stands within view of The Shard, Europe's tallest building, while historic churches designed by Christopher Wren share the horizon with gleaming glass skyscrapers in the financial district.

As the capital of England and the United Kingdom, London serves as a hub for finance, politics, arts, and culture. The Houses of Parliament and Buckingham Palace remain powerful symbols of British governance and monarchy, drawing millions of tourists each year who wish to witness the Changing of the Guard or tour the corridors where centuries of history have unfolded.

The city's cultural institutions are equally impressive. The British Museum houses artifacts spanning human history, while the West End rivals Broadway as a premier destination for theater. London's diverse neighborhoods—from the multicultural streets of Brixton to the trendy shops of Shoreditch—reflect the city's role as a melting pot of global influences.

London's transportation network, including the iconic red double-decker buses and the London Underground (affectionately called "the Tube"), moves millions of commuters daily through a city that never truly sleeps.

Despite challenges including Brexit's economic implications and the lingering effects of the pandemic, London remains a resilient global city, continuing to reinvent itself while honoring its storied past—a true testament to England's enduring influence on the world stage.

# Fashion Diplomacy: Decoding the Style Statements at the Summit

When world leaders gather for high-stakes diplomatic summits, the cameras don't just capture handshakes and policy discussions—they zero in on what's arguably an unofficial competition happening on the sidelines: the fashion choices of political spouses.

This week's international gathering proved no exception, with sartorial choices sparking as much conversation as the summit's actual agenda items.

Several first ladies and spouses opted for a "quiet luxury" approach, favoring monochromatic tailoring over flashy statement pieces. Structured blazers, midi-length skirts, and neutral palettes dominated the official photo lineup, suggesting a coordinated messaging strategy that mirrors the diplomatic tone of the event itself.

Fashion consultants note that this trend toward understated dressing reflects a broader shift in political fashion—away from overt luxury branding and toward pieces that communicate competence and approachability simultaneously.

## Breaking Down the Numbers

While exact price tags are rarely confirmed by official channels, fashion industry analysts have made estimates based on identifiable design details:

- **Tailored ensembles** from recognizable ready-to-wear designers typically range from $2,000-$8,000
- **Custom couture pieces**, when worn, can reach $15,000-$30,000+

Some spouses have drawn praise for deliberately incorporating pieces from their home countries' designers, a move often interpreted as subtle cultural diplomacy that supports domestic fashion industries.

## Sustainability and Repeat-Wear Culture

Interestingly, several spouses were photographed in outfits or accessories worn at previous public engagements—a practice that's increasingly viewed favorably rather than as a fashion faux pas. This "re-wear" trend aligns with growing public sentiment around sustainability, even at the highest levels of international diplomacy.

## The Bigger Picture

Fashion historians point out that spousal style at these events often functions as soft diplomacy—signaling values, cultural respect, and political messaging without a single word being spoken. Color choices sometimes echo host-country flags or themes; silhouette choices can project either approachability or authority depending on the summit's context.
